description: Hi, I’m Amal Dev, a BTech CSE (AI & ML) student currently in 3rd year from Kerala, joining the Trivandrum local event. I’m building a cinematic, scroll-driven Timeline like website that tells the story of NASA hardware left on the Moon, Mars and deep space, made for school-age learners. I work in web development, design and video editing.
summary: sirensofspace is a scroll-driven story website that introduces school-age space fans to 15 retired NASA machines on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. As you scroll, a timeline at the bottom moves from 1967 to 2024, and each machine gets its own animated scene and tells its story in the first person, with real dates and numbers. Visitors meet landers, rovers, probes and a helicopter, such as Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 Eagle, Viking 1, Opportunity, Pioneer 10, Kepler and Ingenuity, and learn why each was sent and what it discovered. The site addresses the challenge by turning dense mission history into a short, engaging story that gives young people a personal connection to these machines and the science they made possible. It is dark, kid-friendly and works on phones.
details:
What it does and how it works: sirensofspace is a scroll-driven story website about 15 retired NASA machines on the Moon, Mars and in deep space: Surveyor 3, Apollo 11 Eagle, ALSEP, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Pioneer 10, Viking 1, Sojourner, NEAR Shoemaker, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Kepler, Dawn, InSight and Ingenuity. Each machine has its own full-screen animated scene. Rovers drive across the screen, landers descend and touch down, probes drift through space, and the helicopter lifts off. A card then fades in with a short first-person story, three key facts with real dates and numbers, and a link to its NASA source page. A timeline fixed at the bottom moves forward through the years from 1967 to 2024 as the visitor scrolls, and its dots jump to each machine.

Benefits and intended impact: The project turns dense mission history into a short, friendly journey for school-age and casual space fans. It aims to give young people a personal connection to these machines and to the science they made possible, so they learn about past missions as well as current ones.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with a canvas starfield and scroll-linked animation. The graphics are drawn with simple shapes. It is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Creativity: The machines tell their own stories in their own voice, and the timeline itself moves with the story.

Factors we considered: Accuracy, since all dates and numbers come from NASA pages with a source link on every card. A kid-friendly tone. A dark, space-like look. Mobile use, so the layout works on phones. Readable text sizes. A small, finished scope of 15 machines done well.
